title: Spiral similarity and the configuration toolkit
blurb: Spiral similarity centres, the Miquel point, symmedians, isogonal conjugates and the mixtilinear incircle, proved and used as tools.
outcomes: Find the centre of a spiral similarity and the Miquel point of four lines
Recognise symmedians and isogonal conjugates and prove their standard properties
Use the incentre-excentre lemma, the shooting lemma and mixtilinear facts in full proofs
lesson:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB\neq AC$. Points $D$ and $E$ move on sides $AB$ and $AC$ so that $BD=CE$. Prove that the circle $ADE$ passes through a fixed point other than $A$. Taking $D=B$, $E=C$ shows the fixed point must lie on the circumcircle $\Gamma$, and an accurate drawing suggests the midpoint $N$ of arc $BAC$. Angle chasing at $N$ does not start, because nothing yet relates $N$ to $D$ and $E$. What relates them is that $N$ is the centre of a rotation taking $D$ to $E$ and $B$ to $C$. This unit develops that view (spiral similarity), its main consequence (the Miquel point), and then four configurations that appear in BMO2 and IMO geometry, namely symmedians, isogonal conjugates, the incentre-excentre lemma and the mixtilinear incircle. Directed angles $\measuredangle$ modulo $180^\circ$ are used as in L4-GE1.

1. Spiral similarity

A spiral similarity with centre $S$, angle $\theta$ and ratio $k>0$ is a rotation about $S$ through $\theta$ followed by the homothety at $S$ with ratio $k$. In complex numbers the map is $z\mapsto s+ke^{i\theta}(z-s)$.

Theorem 1.1. If $A\neq B$, $C\neq D$ and $\overrightarrow{AB}\neq\overrightarrow{CD}$, there is exactly one spiral similarity sending $A$ to $C$ and $B$ to $D$.

Theorem 1.2. In Theorem 1.1, suppose lines $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $X$. Then the centre $S$ is the second intersection of circles $XAB$ and $XCD$ (or $X$ itself, if these circles touch at $X$).

Theorem 1.3. The spiral similarity sending $A\mapsto C$, $B\mapsto D$ and the one sending $A\mapsto B$, $C\mapsto D$ have the same centre.

Proof. For 1.1, the map is $z\mapsto\alpha z+\beta$ with $\alpha=\frac{d-c}{b-a}$ and $\beta=c-\alpha a$. Since $\alpha\neq1$ the map has the fixed point $s=\beta/(1-\alpha)$, and any map sending $a\mapsto c$, $b\mapsto d$ of this form is this one. For 1.3, if $S$ sends $A\mapsto C$, $B\mapsto D$, then $SC/SA=SD/SB$ and $\measuredangle ASC=\measuredangle BSD$, so triangles $SAB$ and $SCD$ are directly similar and so are triangles $SAC$ and $SBD$ (SAS). The second similarity is a spiral similarity at $S$ sending $A\mapsto B$, $C\mapsto D$. For 1.2, from $SAC\sim SBD$, \[\measuredangle SAX=\measuredangle SAC=\measuredangle SBD=\measuredangle SBX,\] so $S,A,B,X$ are concyclic, and similarly $\measuredangle SCX=\measuredangle SDX$ gives $S,C,D,X$ concyclic. If $S=X$ then $X$ is the centre and $AB\parallel CD$, so the circles are homothetic at $X$ and touch there. $\blacksquare$

Solution of the opening problem. Lines $DB$ and $EC$ meet at $A$, so by Theorem 1.2 the centre $M$ of the spiral similarity $D\mapsto B$, $E\mapsto C$ lies on circles $ADE$ and $ABC$. By Theorem 1.3, $M$ is also the centre of the similarity $D\mapsto E$, $B\mapsto C$, whose ratio is $EC/DB=1$. So this similarity is a rotation, and $MB=MC$. Its angle is the angle from $\overrightarrow{DB}$ to $\overrightarrow{EC}$, which is the oriented angle $BAC$, so $M$ sees $BC$ at the same oriented angle as $A$ and $M=N$. (If $AB=AC$ then $DE\parallel BC$, circle $ADE$ touches $\Gamma$ at $A$, and $N=A$. This is why that case is excluded.)

Corollary 1.4. Circles $\omega_1,\omega_2$ meet at $P$ and $Q$. If a line through $P$ meets $\omega_1$ again at $A$ and $\omega_2$ again at $B$, then $Q$ is the centre of a spiral similarity sending $\omega_1$ to $\omega_2$ and $A$ to $B$, the same one for every such line.

Proof. Take two such lines, giving $A,B$ and $A_1,B_1$. The lines $AB$ and $A_1B_1$ joining corresponding points of the similarity $A\mapsto B$, $A_1\mapsto B_1$ meet at $P$, so by Theorem 1.2 its centre is the second intersection of $\omega_1=(PAA_1)$ and $\omega_2=(PBB_1)$, namely $Q$ (the circles meet twice, so they do not touch). This similarity fixes $Q$, so the similarity sends circle $QAA_1=\omega_1$ to circle $QBB_1=\omega_2$. A spiral similarity is determined by its centre and the image of one point, so fixing the first line, every other line gives the same map. $\blacksquare$

Example 1. Circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ meet at $P$ and $Q$. A line through $P$ meets $\omega_1$ again at $A$ and $\omega_2$ again at $B$, and the tangents to $\omega_1$ at $A$ and to $\omega_2$ at $B$ meet at $T$. Prove that $A,B,Q,T$ are concyclic.

With directed angles the tangent-chord angle in $\omega_1$ and in $\omega_2$ gives $\measuredangle(TA,AB)=\measuredangle AQP$ and $\measuredangle(AB,BT)=\measuredangle PQB$, and adding gives $\measuredangle ATB=\measuredangle AQB$. Corollary 1.4 gives a second proof, which shows more. Any line through $A$ and its image under the similarity below meet on circle $ABQ$. The spiral similarity at $Q$ sends $\omega_1$ to $\omega_2$ and $A$ to $B$, so the similarity sends the tangent at $A$ to the tangent at $B$. A spiral similarity with angle $\theta$ turns every line through $\theta$, so $\measuredangle(TA,TB)=\theta=\measuredangle(QA,QB)$. Hence $\measuredangle ATB=\measuredangle AQB$ and the four points are concyclic. (If the tangents are parallel, $\theta=0$, which is impossible since $Q$ is not on line $AB$.)

2. The Miquel point

Theorem 2.1 (Miquel). Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral with no two sides parallel, $Q=AB\cap CD$ and $R=AD\cap BC$. Then circles $QAD$, $QBC$, $RAB$, $RCD$ pass through one point $M$, the Miquel point. This point is the centre of the spiral similarity $A\mapsto B$, $D\mapsto C$ and of the spiral similarity $A\mapsto D$, $B\mapsto C$.

Theorem 2.2. If moreover $ABCD$ is convex and cyclic with centre $O$, then $M$ lies on $QR$, $OM\perp QR$, and $QR^2=QA\cdot QB+RA\cdot RD$.

Proof of 2.1. The map $A\mapsto B$, $D\mapsto C$ is not a translation, as $AB\not\parallel DC$. Lines $AB$ and $DC$ meet at $Q$, so by Theorem 1.2 its centre lies on circles $QAD$ and $QBC$. By Theorem 1.3 the same point is the centre of $A\mapsto D$, $B\mapsto C$, and lines $AD$, $BC$ meet at $R$, so this point lies on circles $RAB$ and $RDC$. (The circles $QAD$, $QBC$ do not touch at $Q$. Then $Q$ would be the centre and would lie on circle $RAB$, which meets line $AB$ only at $A$ and $B$.) $\blacksquare$

Proof of 2.2. From circles $QBCM$ and $RDCM$, \[\measuredangle QMR=\measuredangle QMC+\measuredangle CMR=\measuredangle QBC+\measuredangle CDR=\measuredangle ABC+\measuredangle CDA=0,\] as $ABCD$ is cyclic, so $Q,M,R$ are collinear. Power of $Q$ in circle $RABM$ and of $R$ in circle $QADM$ give $QA\cdot QB=QM\cdot QR$ and $RA\cdot RD=RM\cdot RQ$ (signed along line $QR$). Adding gives $QR^2=QA\cdot QB+RA\cdot RD$. Subtracting, and writing the powers with respect to the circumcircle as $OQ^2-\rho^2$ and $OR^2-\rho^2$, gives $OQ^2-OR^2=MQ^2-MR^2$, so $O$ lies on the perpendicular to $QR$ through $M$. $\blacksquare$

Compare Example 4 of L5-GE1, where the same identity came from Brocard's theorem. In that language $M$ is the inverse of $P=AC\cap BD$ in the circumcircle.

Example 2. Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AD=BC$ and no two sides parallel, and let $Q=AB\cap CD$. Prove that the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $CD$ meet on the circle $QBC$.

Equal lengths $AD=BC$ on two sides suggest a rotation taking one to the other, and its centre would be equidistant from the corresponding endpoints. By Theorem 2.1 the Miquel point $M$ is the centre of the spiral similarity $A\mapsto B$, $D\mapsto C$, whose ratio is $BC/AD=1$. So this similarity is a rotation, and $MA=MB$, $MD=MC$, so $M$ lies on both perpendicular bisectors. These bisectors are not parallel (as $AB\not\parallel CD$), so they meet only at $M$, and $M$ lies on circle $QBC$ by Theorem 2.1.

3. Symmedians

The $A$-symmedian is the reflection of the median $AM$ in the bisector of angle $A$. Two lines through $A$ symmetric in that bisector are called isogonal.

Theorem 3.1. Let the $A$-symmedian meet $BC$ at $L$ and $\Gamma$ again at $K$. (1) $BL/LC=AB^2/AC^2$. (2) $KB/KC=AB/AC$, and $K$ is the only point $X\neq A$ of $\Gamma$ with $XB/XC=AB/AC$. (3) If $\angle A\neq90^\circ$, the tangents to $\Gamma$ at $B$ and $C$ meet on line $AK$. (4) The symmedian bisects every segment $XY$ with $X$ on line $AB$, $Y$ on line $AC$ and $B,C,Y,X$ concyclic (an antiparallel to $BC$).

(1) is the ratio lemma (L4-GE2), which gives $\frac{BL}{LC}=\frac{AB\sin\angle BAL}{AC\sin\angle LAC}$, while for the median $1=\frac{AB\sin\angle BAM}{AC\sin\angle MAC}$. Isogonality swaps the two sines, so $\frac{BL}{LC}=\frac{AB}{AC}\cdot\frac{AB}{AC}$. For (2), $\sin\angle BAK=KB/2R$ and $\sin\angle KAC=KC/2R$, so (1) gives $KB/KC=AB/AC$. The points $X$ with $XB/XC=AB/AC$ form a circle (or the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ if $AB=AC$), which meets $\Gamma$ in at most two points, $A$ and $K$. For (3), let $T$ be the intersection of the tangents and let line $AT$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $K'$. By power of a point $TB^2=TK'\cdot TA$, so triangles $TBK'$ and $TAB$ are similar (common angle at $T$) and $BK'/AB=TB/TA$. Likewise $CK'/AC=TC/TA$. As $TB=TC$, $K'B/K'C=AB/AC$, and $K'=K$ by (2). For (4), reflection in the bisector of angle $A$ turns antiparallels into parallels to $BC$ and the symmedian into the median, which bisects every segment parallel to $BC$. $\blacksquare$

Statement (3) is the form in which symmedians usually appear in problems. You are given the tangents at $B$ and $C$, and you should recognise $AT$ as the symmedian.

Example 3. In triangle $ABC$, the circle through $B$ tangent to line $AC$ at $A$ and the circle through $C$ tangent to line $AB$ at $A$ meet again at $S$. Let $K$ be the reflection of $A$ in $S$. Prove that $K$ lies on $\Gamma$ and that $AK$ is the $A$-symmedian.

The circles touch different lines at $A$, so they cross there and $S\neq A$ exists. The tangent conditions give $\measuredangle(AC,AS)=\measuredangle ABS$ and $\measuredangle(AB,AS)=\measuredangle ACS$, which rearrange to $\measuredangle SBA=\measuredangle SAC$ and $\measuredangle SAB=\measuredangle SCA$. So triangles $SBA$ and $SAC$ are directly similar, and $S$ is the centre of the spiral similarity $B\mapsto A$, $A\mapsto C$. Its angle is $\theta=\measuredangle BSA=\measuredangle SBA+\measuredangle BAS=\measuredangle SAC+\measuredangle BAS=\measuredangle BAC$, and $SB/SA=SA/SC=AB/AC$.

Now $SK=SA=\sqrt{SB\cdot SC}$ and $\measuredangle BSK=\measuredangle BSA=\theta=\measuredangle ASC=\measuredangle KSC$, so triangles $BSK$ and $KSC$ are directly similar (SAS, and as $K$ is on the ray opposite to $SA$, the rotations from ray $SB$ to ray $SK$ and from ray $SK$ to ray $SC$ both equal the angle of the spiral similarity plus $180^\circ$). Hence \[\measuredangle BKC=\measuredangle BKS+\measuredangle SKC=\measuredangle BKS+\measuredangle SBK=\measuredangle BSK=\measuredangle BAC,\] so $K$ lies on $\Gamma$. The same similarity gives $KB/KC=SB/SK=SB/SA=AB/AC$, so $AK$ is the symmedian by Theorem 3.1(2). In particular $S$ is the midpoint of the symmedian chord.

4. Isogonal conjugates

Theorem 4.1. Let $P$ be a point inside triangle $ABC$. The reflections of $AP$, $BP$, $CP$ in the bisectors of the angles at $A$, $B$, $C$ meet at a point $P^*$, the isogonal conjugate of $P$. The six feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ and $P^*$ to the sides lie on one circle, centred at the midpoint of $PP^*$.

Proof. By trigonometric Ceva, \[\frac{\sin\angle BAP}{\sin\angle PAC}\cdot\frac{\sin\angle CBP}{\sin\angle PBA}\cdot\frac{\sin\angle ACP}{\sin\angle PCB}=1.\] Reflecting the three lines swaps the two angles in each fraction, so the product for the reflected lines is the reciprocal, also $1$, and they concur. For the circle, let $F,E$ be the feet from $P$ on $AB,AC$ and $F',E'$ those from $P^*$. Then $AF=AP\cos\angle PAB$, $AE'=AP^*\cos\angle P^*AC=AP^*\cos\angle PAB$, and similarly $AE=AP\cos\angle PAC$, $AF'=AP^*\cos\angle PAC$. So $AF\cdot AF'=AE\cdot AE'$ and $E,E',F,F'$ are concyclic. The midpoint $N$ of $PP^*$ projects onto $AB$ at the midpoint of $FF'$, so $N$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $FF'$, and similarly of $EE'$. This circle has centre $N$. The same holds at $B$, and the two circles share the centre $N$ and the point $F$, so they coincide. $\blacksquare$

The pairs to know are $I\leftrightarrow I$, $O\leftrightarrow H$ (since $\angle BAH=90^\circ-\angle B=\angle OAC$), and the centroid with the symmedian point. For $O$ and $H$ the circle is the nine-point circle.

5. The incentre and the mixtilinear incircle

Write $M_A,M_B,M_C$ for the midpoints of the arcs $BC,CA,AB$ not containing the opposite vertex. Recall the incentre-excentre lemma (L4-GE1), which states $M_AB=M_AC=M_AI=M_AI_A$. The $A$-mixtilinear incircle $\omega_A$ is the circle tangent to $AB$, $AC$ and internally tangent to $\Gamma$. Let $\omega_A$ touch $AB$, $AC$, $\Gamma$ at $K$, $L$, $T$. Since $\omega_A$ lies inside angle $BAC$ and inside $\Gamma$, $T$ is on arc $BC$ not containing $A$.

Theorem 5.1 (shooting lemma). If a circle inside $\Gamma$ touches $\Gamma$ at $T$ and a chord $XY$ at $Z$, then line $TZ$ passes through the midpoint $W$ of arc $XY$ not containing $T$, and $WZ\cdot WT=WX^2$.

Theorem 5.2. (1) $I$ is the midpoint of $KL$. (2) $B,K,I,T$ are concyclic, and so are $C,L,I,T$. (3) Line $TI$ passes through the midpoint $N$ of arc $BAC$.

Proof of 5.1. The homothety at $T$ taking the small circle to $\Gamma$ takes line $XY$ to the tangent of $\Gamma$ parallel to $XY$ on the other side of $XY$ from $T$, and $Z$ to its point of contact, which is $W$. Then $\angle WXZ=\angle WXY=\angle WTX$ (equal arcs $WX$, $WY$), so triangles $WXZ$ and $WTX$ are similar and $WX^2=WZ\cdot WT$. $\blacksquare$

Proof of 5.2. (1) By 5.1 with chord $AB$, $T,K,M_C$ are collinear and $M_CK\cdot M_CT=M_CA^2=M_CI^2$, the last by the incentre-excentre lemma at vertex $C$. So triangles $M_CIK$ and $M_CTI$ are similar, with opposite orientation, and $\measuredangle(IK,IM_C)=\measuredangle(TM_C,TI)$. In the same way $\measuredangle(IM_B,IL)=\measuredangle(TI,TM_B)$. Adding, \[\measuredangle(IK,IL)=\measuredangle M_CTM_B+\measuredangle M_CIM_B=\measuredangle M_CAM_B+\measuredangle M_CIM_B.\] Since $M_BA=M_BI$ and $M_CA=M_CI$, line $M_BM_C$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AI$, so $\measuredangle M_CAM_B=-\measuredangle M_CIM_B$ and $K,I,L$ are collinear. As $AK=AL$ and $AI$ bisects angle $KAL$, $I$ is the midpoint of $KL$ and $KL\perp AI$.

(2) Since triangle $AIK$ has a right angle at $I$, $AK=AI/\cos\tfrac A2=2r/\sin A=bc/s$, which is less than $c$ as $b$ is less than $s$, so $K$ lies on side $AB$. In triangle $BKI$, $\angle BKI=180^\circ-\angle AKI=90^\circ+\tfrac A2$ and $\angle KBI=\tfrac B2$, so $\angle KIB=\tfrac C2$. Also $\angle KTB=\angle M_CTB=\angle M_CCB=\tfrac C2$. As $I$ and $T$ lie on the same side of $AB$, $B,K,I,T$ are concyclic. Similarly for $C,L,I,T$.

(3) By (2), $\measuredangle BTI=\measuredangle BKI=\measuredangle(AB,KL)$ and $\measuredangle ITC=\measuredangle ILC=\measuredangle(KL,AC)$. These are equal, because reflection in $AI$ swaps lines $AB$ and $AC$ and fixes line $KL\perp AI$. So $TI$ bisects angle $BTC$. Triangle $ABC$ lies inside angle $BTC$, so $I$ does and $TI$ is the internal bisector. This bisector passes through the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $T$, which is $N$. $\blacksquare$

Common traps.

  • Pairing points wrongly in Theorem 1.2. The circles contain the two segments being mapped to each other, and $X$ is where the lines joining corresponding points meet.
  • Forgetting the degenerate case of a spiral similarity. A translation has no centre.
  • Calling $AT$ a median, or using Theorem 3.1(3) when $\angle A=90^\circ$ and the tangents are parallel.
  • Using the shooting lemma with the wrong arc midpoint. The right arc is the one on the far side of the chord from $T$.
  • Quoting mixtilinear facts without proof in a BMO2 script. Facts beyond the incentre-excentre lemma should be proved in a few lines.

How to spot this in a contest

  1. Two circles through a common point and a line through that point. The other intersection is a spiral centre (Corollary 1.4).
  2. Four lines, or a quadrilateral with its opposite sides extended. Find the Miquel point before anything else.
  3. Equal lengths on two non-parallel segments suggest a rotation, whose centre is on perpendicular bisectors.
  4. Tangents at $B$ and $C$ meeting at a point give the $A$-symmedian. Equal angles $\angle BAX=\angle YAC$ mean isogonal lines, so look for isogonal conjugates.
  5. An incentre with an arc midpoint, or a circle tangent to two sides and to $\Gamma$ call for the incentre-excentre lemma and Theorems 5.1 and 5.2.

These configurations appear throughout Beyond the Incenter. The cross-ratio chapter there connects Section 3 with harmonic quadrilaterals ($ABKC$ above is one).

practice.q: Triangle $ABC$ has $BC=8$, $CA=9$ and $AB=7$. The $A$-symmedian meets the circumcircle again at $K$. Find $AK$.
practice.hint: Find two similar triangles, one containing the median $AM$ and one containing $AK$.
practice.sol:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Since $AK$ and $AM$ are isogonal, $\angle BAK=\angle MAC$. Also $\angle AKB=\angle ACB=\angle ACM$, as $K$ and $C$ lie on the same side of $AB$ ($K$ is on arc $BC$ not containing $A$). So triangles $ABK$ and $AMC$ are similar, and $AK/AC=AB/AM$, that is, \[AK=\frac{AB\cdot AC}{AM}.\]

By the median formula, $AM^2=\frac{2\cdot 9^2+2\cdot 7^2-8^2}{4}=\frac{196}{4}=49$, so $AM=7$ and $AK=\frac{7\cdot 9}{7}=9$.

practice.q: Circles $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$, with centres $O_1$ and $O_2$, meet at $P$ and $Q$. A line through $P$ meets $\omega_1$ again at $A$ and $\omega_2$ again at $B$. Prove that lines $AO_1$ and $BO_2$ meet at a point of the circle through $Q$, $O_1$ and $O_2$.
practice.hint: The spiral similarity at $Q$ from Corollary 1.4 sends $O_1$ somewhere. Then pair the points differently.
practice.sol:
By Corollary 1.4, the spiral similarity $\sigma$ with centre $Q$ sending $\omega_1$ to $\omega_2$ sends $A$ to $B$. A similarity sends the centre of a circle to the centre of its image, so $\sigma$ sends $O_1$ to $O_2$. By Theorem 1.3, $Q$ is also the centre of the spiral similarity sending $O_1\mapsto A$ and $O_2\mapsto B$.

The angle of $\sigma$ is $\measuredangle O_1QO_2$, which is not $0$ since $Q$ is not on the line of centres. As $\sigma$ sends line $O_1A$ to line $O_2B$, these lines make the angle $\measuredangle O_1QO_2\neq0$ with each other and so meet at a point $X$. Now apply Theorem 1.2 to the similarity $O_1\mapsto A$, $O_2\mapsto B$. The lines joining corresponding points are $O_1A$ and $O_2B$, meeting at $X$, so the centre $Q$ lies on circle $XO_1O_2$. Hence $X$ lies on circle $QO_1O_2$. (If $X=O_1$ or $X=O_2$ the conclusion holds trivially.)

practice.q: Point $P$ lies inside triangle $ABC$ with $\angle PBA=\angle PCA$. Let $D,E,F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ to $BC,CA,AB$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Prove that $D,E,F,M$ lie on a circle.
practice.hint: What does the angle condition say about the isogonal conjugate of $P$?
practice.sol:
Let $P^*$ be the isogonal conjugate of $P$. This point exists and lies inside the triangle by Theorem 4.1, since each reflected line lies inside the corresponding angle. By definition $\angle P^*BC=\angle PBA$ and $\angle P^*CB=\angle PCA$. The hypothesis therefore gives $\angle P^*BC=\angle P^*CB$, so triangle $P^*BC$ is isosceles with $P^*B=P^*C$, and $P^*$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BC$. Hence the foot of the perpendicular from $P^*$ to $BC$ is $M$.

By Theorem 4.1 the feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ and from $P^*$ to the three sides lie on one circle. In particular $D,E,F$ (feet from $P$) and $M$ (a foot from $P^*$) are concyclic. If $M=D$ the statement is about three points and is trivial.

practice.q: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with circumcircle $\Gamma$. The tangents to $\Gamma$ at $B$ and $C$ meet at $T$. Points $D$ on line $AB$ and $E$ on line $AC$ are such that $T$ is the midpoint of $DE$. Prove that $B,C,E,D$ are concyclic.
practice.hint: Construct the antiparallel to $BC$ through $T$, and show that there is only one segment with endpoints on lines $AB$, $AC$ and midpoint $T$.
practice.sol:
Since $\angle A eq90^\circ$, $T$ exists, and by Theorem 3.1(3) line $AT$ is the $A$-symmedian.

Let $t$ be the tangent to $\Gamma$ at $A$ and let $m$ be the line through $T$ parallel to $t$. The line $t$ is not parallel to $AB$ or $AC$, so $m$ meets $AB$ at a point $D_1$ and $AC$ at a point $E_1$. Also $m eq t$, because $T$ is not on $t$ (from $T$ there are only the two tangents $TB$ and $TC$), so $D_1,E_1 eq A$. Further $D_1 eq B$. Otherwise $m=TB$ would be the tangent at $B$ and would be parallel to $t$, so $AB$ would be a diameter and $\angle C=90^\circ$, contrary to the triangle being acute. Similarly $E_1 eq C$.

By the alternate segment theorem $\measuredangle(t,AB)=\measuredangle ACB$, so $\measuredangle(D_1E_1,D_1B)=\measuredangle(t,AB)=\measuredangle ACB=\measuredangle(E_1C,CB)$, which is the directed-angle criterion for $B,C,E_1,D_1$ to be concyclic. So $D_1E_1$ is an antiparallel to $BC$, and by Theorem 3.1(4) the symmedian $AT$ bisects $D_1E_1$. Since $T$ lies on $D_1E_1$, $T$ is its midpoint.

We still need to show $D=D_1$ and $E=E_1$. If $T$ is the midpoint of $DE$, then $E$ is the reflection of $D$ in $T$, so $E$ lies on the reflection of line $AB$ in $T$. That reflection is a line parallel to $AB$, so the reflection meets line $AC$ in exactly one point. Hence $E$, and then $D$, are determined uniquely by the condition, and $(D,E)=(D_1,E_1)$. Therefore $B,C,E,D$ are concyclic.

practice.q: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral in which no two sides are parallel. Lines $AB$ and $CD$ meet at $Q$, and lines $AD$ and $BC$ meet at $R$. Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $QAD$ and $RAB$ meet at a second point $M$, and that $M$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ if and only if \[AB\cdot AD=CB\cdot CD.\]
practice.hint: Show that $M$ is the Miquel point. This point is the centre of two spiral similarities, and the ratio of each can be read off from a pair of opposite sides. Compute $MC/MA$ by going through $MB$.
practice.sol:
First the configuration. No three of $A,B,C,D$ are collinear, so $Q$ is not on line $AD$ (else $Q=A$, and $A$ would lie on line $CD$), and the triangle $QAD$ exists. Similarly triangle $RAB$ exists. By Theorem 2.1 the circles $QAD$, $QBC$, $RAB$, $RCD$ pass through the Miquel point $M_0$ of $ABCD$. Note that $M_0 eq A$. Circle $RCD$ meets line $AD$ only at $R$ and $D$, and $A eq R$ because $R$ lies on line $BC$. The circles $QAD$ and $RAB$ are different, since circle $RAB$ meets line $AD$ only at $R$ and $A$ and so does not contain $D$. Hence they meet at exactly the two points $A$ and $M_0$, and $M=M_0$.

We also need $M$ to differ from each vertex. Circle $QAD$ meets line $AB$ only at $Q,A$ and line $CD$ only at $Q,D$, and $B,C eq Q$, so $M eq B$ and $M eq C$. Circle $RAB$ meets line $AD$ only at $R,A$, and $D eq R$, so $M eq D$. With $M eq A$ from above, the four distances $MA,MB,MC,MD$ are positive.

Now the ratios. By Theorem 2.1, $M$ is the centre of the spiral similarity $\sigma$ with $A\mapsto B$, $D\mapsto C$, and of the spiral similarity $ au$ with $A\mapsto D$, $B\mapsto C$. A spiral similarity with centre $M$ and ratio $k$ multiplies every distance by $k$, distances from $M$ included. The map $\sigma$ sends segment $AD$ to segment $BC$ and $A$ to $B$, so its ratio is \[ rac{BC}{AD}= rac{MB}{MA}.\] The map $ au$ sends segment $AB$ to segment $DC$ and $B$ to $C$, so its ratio is \[ rac{DC}{AB}= rac{MC}{MB}.\] Multiplying the two equations gives, for every quadrilateral in the problem, \[ rac{MC}{MA}= rac{CB\cdot CD}{AB\cdot AD}.\]

Finally, $M$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ if and only if $MA=MC$, that is, if and only if the left side above equals $1$, and this happens if and only if $AB\cdot AD=CB\cdot CD$. Both directions of the equivalence come from the one identity.

The same two ratios give $MB/MD=(BA\cdot BC)/(DA\cdot DC)$ and $MA\cdot MC=MB\cdot MD$. For a cyclic quadrilateral, $\sin\angle BAD=\sin\angle BCD$, so the condition says that triangles $ABD$ and $CBD$ have equal area, that is, $BD$ passes through the midpoint of $AC$. This agrees with Section 2. There $M$ is the inverse of $AC\cap BD$ in the circumcircle, so $M$ lies on the line through the centre and the midpoint of $AC$, which is the perpendicular bisector of $AC$.

practice.q: The $A$-mixtilinear incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches the circumcircle at $T$, and the $A$-excircle touches $BC$ at $X$. With $a=BC$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$ and $s$ the semiperimeter, prove that \[\frac{TB}{TC}=\frac{c(s-b)}{b(s-c)},\] and deduce that $\angle BAT=\angle XAC$.
practice.hint: Use the shooting lemma at $B$ and at $C$, and the two circles $BKIT$, $CLIT$ of Theorem 5.2. Work with sines so that no configuration issues arise.
practice.sol:
Use the notation of Section 5, so $K,L$ are the points of contact on $AB$, $AC$, and $R$ is the circumradius.

Step 1. By the shooting lemma, $T,K,M_C$ are collinear and $M_CK\cdot M_CT=M_CB^2$, so triangles $M_CBK$ and $M_CTB$ are similar and $\frac{BK}{TB}=\frac{M_CB}{M_CT}$. Likewise $\frac{CL}{TC}=\frac{M_BC}{M_BT}$. Hence \[\frac{TB}{TC}=\frac{BK}{CL}\cdot\frac{M_CT}{M_BT}\cdot\frac{M_BC}{M_CB}.\]

Step 2. The chords $M_BC$ and $M_CB$ subtend the angles $\tfrac B2$ and $\tfrac C2$ at $B$ and $C$, so $\frac{M_BC}{M_CB}=\frac{\sin(B/2)}{\sin(C/2)}$. The chord $M_CT$ subtends $\angle M_CCT=\angle ICT$ at $C$ (as $I$ lies on segment $CM_C$), and $M_BT$ subtends $\angle IBT$ at $B$. In circle $CLIT$, $\sin\angle ICT=\sin\angle ILT$, and in circle $BKIT$, $\sin\angle IBT=\sin\angle IKT$ (inscribed angles on the same chord are equal or supplementary). As $I$ lies on segment $KL$, the sine rule in triangle $TKL$ gives \[\frac{M_CT}{M_BT}=\frac{\sin\angle ILT}{\sin\angle IKT}=\frac{\sin\angle KLT}{\sin\angle LKT}=\frac{TK}{TL}.\]

Step 3. Let $\rho_1,\rho_2$ be the radii of circles $BKIT$ and $CLIT$. Then $TK=2\rho_1\sin\angle TBA$ and $TL=2\rho_2\sin\angle TCA$, and these sines are equal because $ABTC$ is cyclic. So $\frac{TK}{TL}=\frac{\rho_1}{\rho_2}$. In the proof of Theorem 5.2 we found $\angle KIB=\tfrac C2$, and similarly $\angle LIC=\tfrac B2$, so $\rho_1=\frac{BK}{2\sin(C/2)}$, $\rho_2=\frac{CL}{2\sin(B/2)}$ and \[\frac{TK}{TL}=\frac{BK}{CL}\cdot\frac{\sin(B/2)}{\sin(C/2)}.\]

Step 4. Combining, $\frac{TB}{TC}=\left(\frac{BK}{CL}\right)^2\frac{\sin^2(B/2)}{\sin^2(C/2)}$. From Theorem 5.2, $AK=AL=bc/s$, so $BK=\frac{c(s-b)}{s}$ and $CL=\frac{b(s-c)}{s}$. The half-angle formulas give $\sin^2\tfrac B2=\frac{(s-a)(s-c)}{ac}$ and $\sin^2\tfrac C2=\frac{(s-a)(s-b)}{ab}$. Therefore \[\frac{TB}{TC}=\frac{c^2(s-b)^2}{b^2(s-c)^2}\cdot\frac{b(s-c)}{c(s-b)}=\frac{c(s-b)}{b(s-c)}.\]

Step 5. Let $x=\angle BAT$, so $\angle TAC=A-x$, as $T$ lies on arc $BC$ not containing $A$. By the extended sine rule $\frac{\sin x}{\sin(A-x)}=\frac{TB}{TC}$. Let $y=\angle XAC$. Since $BX=s-c$ and $XC=s-b$, the ratio lemma gives $\frac{s-c}{s-b}=\frac{c\sin(A-y)}{b\sin y}$, so $\frac{\sin y}{\sin(A-y)}=\frac{c(s-b)}{b(s-c)}=\frac{\sin x}{\sin(A-x)}$. The function $t\mapsto\frac{\sin t}{\sin(A-t)}$ is increasing on $(0,A)$, since its derivative is $\frac{\sin A}{\sin^2(A-t)}>0$. Hence $x=y$, that is, $\angle BAT=\angle XAC$.
